body: Oil Traders Want U.S. to Release Sanctioned Tankers as Freight Costs Soar Haley Zaremba is an energy journalist and researcher with more than a decade of professional experience covering global energy systems, land and natural resources, and… As we head into the United Nations’ 31st annual flagship climate conference (COP31), to be held next week in Antalya, Türkiye, greenwashing presents a large and growing problem in the private sector. As the tech sector’s greenhouse gas emissions explode against the backdrop of the artificial intelligence boom and the clean energy incentives dry up under the Trump administration, Big Tech and Wall Street alike are funding a boom in natural gas, all under the guise of funding the future of clean energy. “ On Wall Street, the ‘energy transition’ includes natural gas and data centers ,” blared a Grist headline published earlier this week. The article details how private equity funds are making a killing on “energy transition” funds as electrification takes hold on a global scale and solar and wind power continue to see runaway growth trends, both current and projected. But many of these prominent energy transition funds prominently feature a fossil fuel and major contributors to greenhouse gas emissions on a global scale: natural gas. “‘Energy transition’ is a flexible term,” says Dan Cohn, an energy finance analyst with the energy think tank Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. “And I’m unsurprised to see either the gas or electrical equipment and data center-related companies in some of these funds. That is perfectly consistent with how I know some investors think about the energy transition,” he went on to say. And those investors are not alone. Natural gas has been heavily promoted by the fossil fuel sector as a ‘bridge fuel’, serving as a stepping stone in the transition away from oil and coal toward 100 percent renewables. However, environmental experts question the wisdom of this approach and scientists have pushed back on the idea that natural gas is any cleaner than other fossil fuels, and calls for the abandonment of the ‘bridge fuel’ narrative have gained momentum in recent years. Methane, the principal ingredient in natural gas, is an extremely potent greenhouse gas. While methane breaks up much more quickly in the atmosphere than the better-known carbon dioxide, it is 80 times more potent at warming over a 20-year period. And peer–reviewed studies (like this one , this one , and this one ) are increasingly indicating that natural gas produces much, much more methane over its life cycle than previously thought. Plus, some studies even indicate that natural gas could be worse for the climate than coal when you include the emissions associated with the energy-intensive cooling, storage, and shipping processes associated with liquefied natural gas. However, the ‘bridge fuel’ argument still seems to hold major currency on Wall Street and in Silicon Valley. “I know a lot of the investors out there do consider gas a transition fuel,” Ryan Loughead, a senior associate and former climate solutions analyst for BloombergNEF, told Grist. For example, New York-based Blackstone, one of the world’s largest private equity firms, “is explicit in its view that methane gas, a fossil fuel and the primary component of natural gas, is essential to the energy transition,” reports Grist. Meanwhile, Big Tech firms are causing a major natural gas boom around the country at the same time that they tout their backing of next-gen clean energy research, development, and adoption. Some of the biggest names in tech are building historically huge natural gas plants as we speak. Amazon is constructing a gas-fired power plant in Texas that will be the single-biggest source of power-related emissions in the entire United States according to current specs, which include seven gas plants. title: Copper faces further slide after US vote: TD
summary: Copper could fall further as Democratic Party gains in the United States midterm elections weaken expectations for import tariffs.
body: Copper could fall further as Democratic Party gains in the United States midterm elections weaken expectations for import tariffs and raise doubts about projected demand from data centres, TD Securities says. Three-month copper futures on the London Metal Exchange declined to about $13,779 per tonne, or $6.25 per lb., by late afternoon Friday in London, their lowest level since July, data show. The metal has retreated from September’s intraday peak of almost $6.80 per lb. as traders reassess demand and the incentive to accumulate U.S. stockpiles. “We continue to expect the red metal to face further downside from here,” TD Securities managing director and global head of commodity strategy Bart Melek said in a note published Thursday. The risk is that copper loses some of the support from U.S. stockpiling before expected growth in data-centre consumption materializes. Mine disruptions and tight supplies outside the U.S. could nevertheless limit the decline, Fitch Group’s BMI research and data unit says. Democratic gains could increase resistance to power-hungry data centres, a source of expected copper demand growth, TD says. Affordability concerns ahead of the 2028 presidential vote could also reduce the appetite for aggressive copper tariffs, it says. “With many states slated for significant AI data center development turning blue, and opposition to new construction potentially growing, AI-driven copper demand could fall meaningfully short of current projections,” Melek wrote. “At the same time, many traders believe aggressive copper tariffs are now less likely with the Democratic Party controlling the U.S. Congress, and affordability the Achilles’ heel for the governing party heading into 2028.” U.S. copper inventories total about 1.6 million tonnes, TD estimates. Reduced stockpiling incentives and the disappearance of profitable price differences between American and overseas markets could halt additional inflows for a significant period. Slower imports would not necessarily mean an equivalent decline in industrial consumption. “As such, another $500 per tonne drift lower would not be a major surprise,” Melek wrote. Based on Thursday’s closing copper price of $13,843 per tonne in London, that would represent a drop of about 3.6%. BMI also sees tariff policy as the immediate catalyst, although it expects mine constraints and electrification demand to cushion any correction. It expects copper to average $13,500 per tonne this year and $12,900 in 2027. “U.S. tariff uncertainty remains the clearest near-term catalyst for copper, in our view,” BMI said in a report published Thursday. Washington’s July 2025 copper proclamation outlined possible refined copper duties of 15% from January 2027, rising to 30% in 2028, subject to a subsequent presidential determination. While Democratic gains could increase political pressure over the decision, the proclamation leaves it with the president — and the proposed levies remain unenacted. Separate 50% duties on certain semi-finished copper products and copper-intensive derivative products took effect in August 2025. Anticipation has nevertheless redirected trade. Higher Comex prices relative to London encouraged shipments into American warehouses before potential tariffs, reducing metal available elsewhere. Comex inventories rose about 62% from January through Wednesday, BMI reported, with those warehouses holding about 70% of global exchange copper stocks on Oct. 30. The dislocation overlays a concentrated supply chain. Chile supplied 68% of U.S. refined copper imports during 2021–24, followed by Canada at 16%, U.S. Geological Survey data show. China produced an estimated 14 million tonnes of refined copper in 2025, nearly half the global total. Chinese buyers are paying more to secure immediately available metal. body: Gold pulled back on Friday to test a trend support zone, establishing a lower daily high of $4,107 and a low of $4,027. This followed bullish signals from Thursday, including a reclaim of the 20-day moving average and downtrend line, plus a breakout above the recent lower swing high of $4,082 on the daily chart, which also represented a bullish reversal signal on the weekly chart. A higher weekly low was also generated this week at $3,875, supporting the potential for the beginning of a reversal in the current decline. The bullish signal was confirmed with a close above each of the resistance levels. Fridayâs pullback now provides an opportunity to assess whether those former resistance levels will hold as support. Since the recent decline took the form of a parallel trend channel, a breakout from that pattern also triggered on Thursday. The breakout hit resistance at $4,147 and closed in the lower half of the dayâs range, indicating that sellers were beginning to take control and raising the potential for a pullback to test prior resistance as support. That dynamic continued Friday. Bullish momentum that led to the breakout began from the recent low of $3,870, with a 7.15% advance completed at Thursdayâs high. That exceeded the previous three upswings that occurred since the August swing high at $4,697, the largest of which was an advance of 5.33%. This adds to the bullish technical evidence that buyers may be reclaiming control. It also suggests that by the time the prior swing high was recovered, gold was extended and prone to at least a small correction. This bullish price behavior indicates that the $3,870 low may have completed the corrective decline from the August high. If gold falls below Fridayâs low of $4,027, it could decline further to test support near the 61.8% Fibonacci retracement at $3,975, which is reinforced by a previous swing low. However, since the upside breakout signal from Thursday was confirmed with a close above the range, a recovery and continuation of the bullish reversal process is anticipated. Kitco provides the live gold price in U.S. dollars from the global spot market, updated every few seconds during trading hours. The table below breaks today's gold spot price in U.S. dollars into the units used in bullion and jewelry trade, converted live from the per-troy-ounce quote. Prices in U.S. dollars, based on the bid price of the global spot market. Tael refers to the Hong Kong tael (37.799 g). The spot price is the market price for one troy ounce of gold for immediate delivery, quoted in U.S. dollars. It is derived from the most actively traded gold futures contract together with over-the-counter dealing, and it moves nearly around the clock as trading follows the sun from New York to London, Zurich, Shanghai and Hong Kong. A troy ounce is 31.1034768 grams — about 10% heavier than the avoirdupois ounce used for groceries. Physical bullion products trade at a premium above spot that covers fabrication and distribution; the premium is proportionally larger on small items than on large bars. The chart above tracks this spot price. The currency selector converts the same underlying quote into other currencies using live exchange rates. The spot price is for gold delivered now; a futures price is for gold delivered on a set date in the future, traded on exchanges such as COMEX. The two normally differ by the cost of carrying gold to that date — storage, insurance and interest — which is why futures usually trade slightly above spot, a condition called contango . When futures trade below spot — backwardation — it signals unusually strong demand for immediate physical delivery, and it’s rare enough in gold that it makes news when it happens. The price on this page is the spot price; quotes you see for "gold futures" refer to the most active COMEX contract. Real interest rates and the Federal Reserve. Gold pays no yield, so its strongest headwind is a high real (inflation-adjusted) interest rate — and its strongest tailwind is a falling one. Fed rate decisions, inflation reports and Treasury yields are the events most likely to move the gold price on any given day. Inflation and currency debasement. Gold's reputation as an inflation hedge is best understood over long horizons: across decades, gold has broadly preserved purchasing power as paper currencies lost it, which is why demand rises when investors expect sustained inflation or growing government debt. Over shorter periods the relationship is looser — in an inflation spike, what matters most is how the Fed responds, which is why real interest rates (above) are the better day-to-day guide. The U.S. dollar. Gold is priced in dollars, so a weaker dollar tends to lift the gold price and a stronger dollar tends to weigh on it — even when nothing about gold itself has changed. To see how much of a move is gold versus the dollar, the Kitco Global Index (KGX) tracks gold’s value measured against a basket of major currencies with the U.S. dollar’s influence stripped out. body: Brent crude oil is heading for its biggest weekly percentage decline since the COVID-19 pandemic, with prices falling approximately 16% as investors increasingly anticipate a de-escalation of the US-Israeli war against Iran. January Brent futures traded near $98.60 per barrel at 11:29 GMT, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) hovered around $91. Brent's projected weekly decline would also be its largest in dollar terms in LSEG records dating to 1988. However, the weekly figures remain provisional until trading closes. The selloff accelerated after the November 3 US midterm elections, when Democrats won both chambers of Congress. Investors interpreted the result as increasing political pressure for a negotiated settlement with Iran, potentially allowing additional Gulf oil exports to return to international markets. Brent plunged more than 8% on Wednesday alone, reaching a two-month low near $94.62. The move followed an earlier decline below $103 , when President Donald Trump indicated that Washington had no immediate plans for additional strikes. Oil's reversal is particularly dramatic because Brent traded above $116 in late October following tanker attacks near the Strait of Hormuz . That earlier rally reflected fears of prolonged export disruptions rather than an immediate shortage of equivalent size. As Coinpaper explained in its analysis of oil prices and OPEC supply , futures markets respond to expected supply conditions, not simply barrels currently available. Despite falling prices, the Middle East's physical supply risks have not disappeared. Britain's maritime security agency UKMTO reported that attacks on oil-carrying vessels remained close to record levels. A seafarer was killed following an explosion aboard an oil-products tanker, while further incidents renewed concerns about shipping safety. The disruptions follow earlier US strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island , which temporarily pushed crude prices higher. Meanwhile, OPEC+ agreed to maintain September's required production levels for December rather than announce another increase. The decision reinforces the distinction between official output targets and oil actually reaching buyers. Earlier Iran peace negotiations and the OPEC+ production freeze demonstrated how quickly diplomatic expectations can outweigh production decisions. Brent's immediate resistance sits around $100, followed by $103–$105 if prices sustain a recovery. However, a stronger rebound toward $110 would likely require renewed supply concerns or a significant deterioration in negotiations. title: Sell-Side Analysts Fail To Adequately Adjust Stock Forecasts After Fed Meetings - Eurasia Review
body: When the U.S. Federal Reserve announces a change in its interest rate, consumers expect shifts in borrowing costs elsewhere and potential price adjustments for things like housing and some consumer goods. New research however shows that stock market analysts generally give a collective “meh” around the time of Fed meetings when it comes to forecasting how much stocks will trade for in the future, called a price target. Despite dozens of Fed meetings between 2000 and 2020 where interest rates were either raised or lowered, researchers at the University of Toronto’s Rotman School of Management found that price targets among analysts working at investment houses and brokerages were only adjusted for 18.5 percent of companies in the two weeks before and after Fed meetings. As a result, those targets — which investors use when deciding to buy or sell stocks — lose accuracy after a Fed meeting, either overpredicting future stock prices when rates rise or underpredicting them when rates drop. In practice, stock prices on average fall in response to interest rate hikes and rise when rates relax. Comparing actual stock prices to what was forecast, the researchers found that prediction inaccuracy increased by about 13 percent when the Fed hiked rates and by more than 16 percent when rates dropped. That analysts are making such mistakes is “not surprising,” said lead author Junhao Liu, a senior accounting lecturer, which is equivalent to an assistant professor, at the University of Melbourne who conducted the research while completing his PhD in the Rotman School’s accounting doctoral program. “Analysts always make mistakes, whether intentional or unintentional.” The driver of this particular error, show Dr. Liu and his co-researchers, is a failure to adjust the discount rate analysts use as part of their forecasting. Expressed as a percentage, the discount rate accounts for things like risk, interest rates and the cost of tying up money over the longer term and translates a stock’s future value into today’s money. Not surprisingly, forecast inaccuracy was heightened for companies with high exposure to interest rates, such as financial and highly leveraged companies. It was less pronounced for investment houses with macro-economists on staff who presumably could provide more precise guidance on potential impacts of interest rate changes. Even having highly rated crackerjack analysts did not help after a Fed rate increase, which happened 29 times during the studied period. Those hot performers did however show less inaccuracy around rate decreases, which happened 28 times. The findings highlight “potential limitations in how some of the most important capital market intermediaries interpret and act upon fundamental macroeconomic information,” said Ole-Kristian Hope, who is the Deloitte Professor of Accounting at the Rotman School who supervised Dr. Liu’s research. The study was also co-authored by Rotman accounting PhD graduate Mingyue Zhang, now an assistant professor in financial reporting at the University of Waterloo. While the research did not delve into why analysts fall short in adjusting their target prices, Dr. Liu speculated that it may be because they are just being conservative — not wanting to make changes because these will have consequences elsewhere — may be unable to process the exact effect of the interest rate change, or they may feel incentivized to maintain high price forecasts in the face of an interest rate hike. Given the wild rise in interest rates following the COVID-19 pandemic, the findings could be helpful to investors trying to make sense of the market and to analysts striving for better accuracy in an era of dramatic monetary policy shifts, the research concludes.
